items.headline: Thinking Machines releases Inkling, a 975B open-weights multimodal MoE
items.diff_narrative: A net-new model release that sits at the opposite end of the scale axis from yesterday's lead. Bonsai 27B carried the slate by shrinking a 27B-class model to 3.9 GB so it fits inside a phone's memory budget; Inkling is a 975B-total / 41B-active Mixture-of-Experts pretrained from scratch on 45 trillion tokens of text, images, audio, and video with a context window up to 1M tokens, released as open weights by Mira Murati's Thinking Machines Lab on July 15 alongside a 276B-total Inkling-Small preview. What connects the two days is the business logic rather than the parameter count: where PrismML paid a 5-10% benchmark tax to cross a hardware threshold, Thinking Machines concedes outright that Inkling is not the strongest model available and bets instead that enterprises want a customizable base routed into its Tinker fine-tuning platform rather than a rented frontier endpoint. Together AI served the model on day 0 behind an OpenAI-compatible endpoint, and the release makes a second US neolab — after the summer's Chinese MoE wave — put frontier-scale trained-from-scratch weights into the open with fine-tuning as the explicit business model.

items.headline: Unsloth v0.1.49-beta ships same-day Inkling support and a four-level tool-call permission system
items.diff_narrative: A new tooling item that threads yesterday's two dominant registers — open-weight model support and agent-tooling security — through a single release. Unsloth's v0.1.49-beta, published July 15, lands Inkling support in the same news cycle as the model itself, but the diff-relevant change is the security surface: a four-level tool-call permission selector (Ask, Approve for me, Off, Full access) with workspace isolation replaces the previous binary toggle. Yesterday's slate documented what happens when agent tooling lacks that vocabulary — the Grok CLI shipping working trees to a cloud bucket by default, Cursor executing unvalidated binaries on folder open — and today a fine-tuning framework adopts the permission-gating grammar that coding agents converged on after this year's exfiltration incidents. Hardware reach also widens, with Intel GPUs gaining Vulkan-backed llama.cpp inference where they were previously CPU-bound, extending the NVFP4/FP8 export path from v0.1.48.

items.headline: Microsoft's record 570-CVE Patch Tuesday carries a critical Copilot RCE cluster
items.diff_narrative: The security slot pivots from disclosure politics to patch volume. Yesterday's security items were about process failures — Mindgard publishing an unpatched Cursor flaw after seven months of vendor silence, and a wire-level teardown proving the Grok CLI's default upload path — where the vulnerabilities themselves were single and mundane. Today's item is the opposite shape: Microsoft's July 14 Patch Tuesday fixed a record 570 vulnerabilities including three zero-days, and the AI surface is now a recurring category rather than an exotic one-off — a critical remote-code-execution flaw in Microsoft Copilot itself (CVE-2026-48561), a GitHub Copilot RCE, a Copilot / VS Code security-feature bypass, and a Copilot / VS Code token-disclosure flaw. The volume is itself an AI story on both sides of the ledger: Microsoft attributes the surge to its AI-powered internal vulnerability-discovery system, and Adobe moved to twice-monthly bulletins the same day, citing AI-accelerated discovery compressing the disclosure-to-exploitation window — the structural pressure yesterday's Mindgard embargo-break was an early symptom of.

items.headline: xAI open-sources the entire Grok Build coding agent after the wire-level upload teardown
items.diff_narrative: A direct sequel to yesterday's lead security item, and the rare case where a disclosure gets an answer within the same news window. Yesterday's slate carried the mitmproxy capture showing the Grok build CLI shipping entire repositories, git history, and unredacted .env secrets to a Google Cloud bucket; today xAI responds by publishing the whole agent as xai-org/grok-build under Apache 2.0 — 844,530 lines of Rust, roughly 97% original code, exported from the internal monorepo — with the offending upload path disabled outright, its remnant Google Cloud code now returning hardcoded unavailability errors. The teardown's open question about what the binary does is answered by making the binary inspectable: Simon Willison's read-through surfaces the full agent and subagent system prompts, tool implementations ported from competing agents including Codex and Claude Code, and a codebase materially larger than the terminal-agent norm. Against yesterday's other disclosure thread — Mindgard's seven months of Cursor vendor silence — this is the strongest disclosure-driven outcome of the year's agent-trust incidents: full source publication rather than a changelog apology.

items.headline: TSMC posts a record quarter on AI demand as 2nm reaches its first reported wafer revenue
items.diff_narrative: The business slot swaps an authenticity audit for an audited financial record. Yesterday's business item was the x402 measurement showing a fifth of 136.7 million agent-payment settlements were fictitious — a caution that headline adoption numbers can be manufactured. Today's number is the opposite kind: TSMC's July 16 second-quarter results are a regulated filing quantifying real AI demand — revenue of US$40.20 billion up 36.0% year-over-year, net income up 77.4%, and margins of 67.7% gross and 55.6% net that would have been implausible for a foundry two years ago. The forward signal is the node mix: 2-nanometer contributed 3% of wafer revenue in its first meaningful quarter, Q3 guidance of US$44.6-45.8 billion rides the 2nm ramp, and the 2026 capital-spending plan rises to US$60-64 billion. For the threads that ran through earlier slates — accelerator allocations, hyperscaler build schedules, and the on-device NPU roadmaps that yesterday's Bonsai 27B release targets — the constraint picture is unchanged: demand is rationed by wafer supply, and TSMC is spending accordingly.

items.headline: AI events calendar: OpenAI DevDay and PyTorch Conference join, AGI Summit decision now days away
items.diff_narrative: The roster carries forward intact — the AGI Summit still leads at the Palace of Fine Arts this weekend, AMD Advancing AI on July 22-23, the July 31 Hot Chips early-rate deadline, the early-August Las Vegas security block, and the autumn run through GitHub Universe, re:Invent, and NeurIPS — with yesterday's two embodied-AI additions, the Runway AI Summit and IEEE-RAS Humanoids, now folded into the standing list. Two additions change the September calculus: OpenAI DevDay 2026 lands Tuesday, September 29 at Fort Mason in San Francisco — in-person applications already closed, keynote streaming free, DevDay Exchanges following in eight cities — which stacks the same date as The AI Conference's opening at Pier 48 and the eve of the Runway AI Summit into one San Francisco super-week and forces a pick-a-lane decision; and PyTorch Conference North America 2026 takes October 20-21 in San Jose with vLLM, DeepSpeed, and Ray coverage and discounted early registration open now. The nearest action tightens from before Saturday to a matter of days: the AGI Summit opens July 18.
